items.body:
The e2e test framework has several patterns that cause flakiness, silent resource leaks, and hard-to-debug failures, especially in disruptive tests that restart API servers or control plane components. PR 137832 addresses these across 13 files (185 additions, 41 deletions), touching SIG api-machinery, apps, cloud-provider, network, node, storage, and testing.

Error suppression hides resource leaks. Across the test suite, cleanup code discards errors from Delete calls. In test/e2e/apimachinery/aggregator.go, the cleanupSampleAPIServer function has 10 such calls (APIService, Deployment, Secret, Service, ServiceAccount, RoleBinding, ClusterRoleBinding, ClusterRole) all silently swallowed. Same pattern in test/e2e/apimachinery/apply.go (4 deployments/pods), test/e2e/apps/rc.go (DeleteCollection), and test/e2e/apps/statefulset.go (ConfigMaps in defer blocks). When these fail, resources leak into subsequent tests with zero trace of what went wrong.

No retry on transient API server errors. GetControlPlaneNodes in test/e2e/framework/util.go calls Nodes().List() and immediately fails on any error. During disruptive tests (daemon restarts, etcd failure injection), the API server is expected to be briefly unreachable. The same issue exists in allNodesReady at test/e2e/framework/node/helper.go and RestartNodes at test/e2e/common/util.go. A transient connection refused or 503 kills the entire test instead of retrying. The fix introduces IsRetryableAPIError which checks for connection refused/reset, server timeout, 429, 503, 500, and unexpected server errors, plus a new WaitForControlPlaneNodes that wraps the listing in a polling loop with retry-on-transient logic.

Healthz returns 200 before daemon is ready. RestartDaemonConfig.waitUp in test/e2e/apps/daemon_restart.go considers the daemon ready when /healthz returns HTTP 200. After a kubelet restart, the health endpoint can report ok while kubelet is still recovering. Logs show errors, pods are not yet scheduled. The fix adds verifyDaemonReadiness which SSHes into the node and checks the last 20 lines of /var/log/kubelet.log for error patterns before declaring readiness.

Goroutines not gracefully stopped. In test/e2e/apps/daemon_restart.go, a cache.NewInformer controller is started with go controller.Run(backgroundCtx.Done()). The cleanup calls cancel() but does not wait for the controller goroutine to finish. The fix replaces this with a dedicated stopCh channel and DeferCleanup that closes the channel then sleeps 100ms to allow graceful shutdown.

PVC deletion races with pod references. DeleteAllStatefulSets in test/e2e/framework/statefulset/rest.go has a TODO comment about not checking whether pods still reference PVCs before deleting them. The current code deletes PVCs immediately, which can fail or leave orphaned PVs when pods are still running. The fix lists pods, checks volume references, and only deletes PVCs that are not in use, with foreground propagation.

Duplicated control plane filtering. GetControlPlaneNodes and WaitForControlPlaneNodes both contain the same node filtering logic (check for control-plane label and NoSchedule taint). The second commit extracts this into a shared filterControlPlaneNodes helper.

All changes are in e2e test code, no user-facing impact.

Related issues:
- 109600: prevent the Expect(err).NotTo(HaveOccurred()) and ExpectNoError(err) anti-pattern in e2e tests (same category of error handling problems)
- 86253: sample-apiserver returns error instead of falling back to second Accept type (directly affects the aggregator.go test modified in this PR)
- 135285: GOAWAY are not handled gracefully in apiserver when aggregating (related network error handling)
- 105536: Orphaned pod found, but error not a directory occurred when trying to remove the volumes dir (related resource cleanup issue)

items.body:
<!-- This issue was generated with AI assistance -->

## What happened?

The `validateParallelismChange` admission check in `plugin/pkg/admission/job/admission.go` uses an AND condition to skip validation:

```go
if !p.genericWorkloadEnabled && !p.workloadWithJobEnabled {
    return nil
}
```

This means the gang-scheduling parallelism guard is active when **either** feature gate is enabled. Disabling only `WorkloadWithJob` (or only `GenericWorkload`) is not sufficient to bypass the check — both must be disabled.

If a user disables `WorkloadWithJob` expecting to opt out of gang-scheduling admission behavior, the check still fires because `GenericWorkload` is enabled (or vice versa).

## What did you expect to happen?

Disabling the relevant feature gate for the code path being exercised should be sufficient to skip the validation. For example, the `SchedulingGroup`-based path (line 133) only makes sense with `GenericWorkload`, and the owner-reference scan path (line 148) only makes sense with `WorkloadWithJob`. Each branch should be gated independently on its corresponding feature gate, rather than both branches being gated on the OR of the two gates.

## How can we reproduce it?

1. Disable `WorkloadWithJob` feature gate, leave `GenericWorkload` enabled.
2. Create a Job that has an owner-created PodGroup with gang scheduling.
3. Attempt to update the Job's parallelism.
4. Observe `is forbidden: cannot change parallelism for a Job referencing gang-scheduled PodGroup` even though `WorkloadWithJob` is disabled.

## Relevant code

`plugin/pkg/admission/job/admission.go`, `validateParallelismChange` function.

items.title: CronJob controller: processNextWorkItem does not call queue.Forget on the  (nil, nil) sync path, leaving stale rate-limiter backoff count

labels.name: sig/apps
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Apps.

labels.name: triage/accepted
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR is ready to be actively worked on.

items.body:
/sig apps

**Description**

In `pkg/controller/cronjob/cronjob_controllerv2.go#processNextWorkItem` only resets the workqueue rate limiter (queue.Forget) inside the requeueAfter != nil branch. When sync() returns (nil, nil) — no error and no requeue — none of the switch branches run, so Forget is never called:

```
requeueAfter, err := jm.sync(ctx, key)
switch {
case err != nil:
    utilruntime.HandleError(...)
    jm.queue.AddRateLimited(key)
case requeueAfter != nil:
    jm.queue.Forget(key)
    jm.queue.AddAfter(key, *requeueAfter)
// err == nil && requeueAfter == nil: nothing runs, Forget is not called
}

return true

```

Some paths/conditions when nil, nil are returned are such as below:
- CronJob not found / already deleted (returned directly by sync)
- CronJob being deleted (DeletionTimestamp != nil)
- CronJob suspended (spec.suspend == true)
- invalid spec.timeZone
- unparseable or invalid spec.schedule


**Issue**
I took one example flow and say : 
Take a suspended CronJob: on any given sync it may or may not need a status write, and that write may or may not succeed.( in `pkg/controller/cronjob/cronjob_controllerv2.go#syncCronJob` )
- Status write fails → sync returns (nil, err) → processNextWorkItem takes the err != nil branch → AddRateLimited increments the failure count.
- Status write succeeds → sync returns (nil, nil) → no branch runs → the count is left unchanged.

So the same path that can drive the counter up (when its status write errors) never brings it back down (when its status write succeeds).


**What happens if this isn't fixed**

I would be honest, i dont want to oversell this and the severity/impact might be on the lower side but there is definitely an impact.

Consider a CronJob that accumulated some failures during an API incident and is then suspended . Because the suspended sync returns (nil, nil), the stale failure count is retained. When the CronJob is later resumed and its first reconcile hits a transient error, AddRateLimited computes the backoff from the stale count rather than from a clean baseline.
Also - since queue keys by namespace/name, a later CronJob recreated with the same name inherits the previous object's stale backoff.

**Potential Fix**
Its just a simple one liner.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/139918

**How was this uncovered**

In the sprit of full transparency :

I found this while building my own open source case study [tool](https://github.com/somak2kai/beats) on golang structural fingerprints and potential outliers and I used Kubernetes (among many others oss repos) as test subjects.  
processNextWorkItem in cronjob_controllerv2 was marked as a potential outlier compared to its cousins  such as the below ( and all of the below follow similar pattern of .forget on queue)
certificates/clustertrustbundlepublisher/publisher.go#processNextWorkItem
processNextWorkItem	rootcacertpublisher	certificates/rootcacertpublisher/publisher.go#processNextWorkItem
controller/bootstrap/tokencleaner.go#processNextWorkItem
controller/certificates/certificate_controller.go#processNextWorkItem

The goal of the tool was not to find issues , but was to perform a case study. This particular issue stood out , hence raising it. No personal agenda behind this 🙏

items.title: PDB maxUnavailable cannot compute expectedPods when a pod's direct controller owner does not implement /scale but a scalable ancestor exists

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: sig/apps
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Apps.

labels.name: needs-triage
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR lacks a `triage/foo` label and requires one.

items.body:
## What happened

The disruption controller computes `expectedPods` for a PDB using `maxUnavailable` by calling the `/scale` subresource on each matched pod's **direct** controller owner (`metav1.GetControllerOf(pod)` → scale lookup in `pkg/controller/disruption/disruption.go`, `getExpectedScale` / `getPodControllerFromScale`).

When the direct owner does not implement `/scale`, the lookup errors and the PDB falls back to `expectedPods: 0` → `disruptionsAllowed: 0`, emitting:

```
Warning  CalculateExpectedPodCountFailed
  Failed to calculate the number of expected pods:
  <resource> does not implement the scale subresource
```

This blocks **all** voluntary evictions for the protected pods, even when a *scalable* resource exists higher in the ownership chain.

## Why this matters beyond one project

This is a general limitation for any operator/CRD pattern with multi-level ownership, where the immediately-owning object is a per-instance (non-scalable) resource but a higher-level controller is scalable. A concrete, widely-deployed example is KubeVirt:

```
virt-launcher Pod  →  VirtualMachineInstance   (direct owner, NOT scalable)
                   →  VirtualMachine
                   →  VirtualMachinePool        (scalable — implements /scale)
```

`VirtualMachinePool` implements `/scale`, but the disruption controller never reaches it because it stops at the direct owner (`VirtualMachineInstance`). Result: `maxUnavailable` PDBs are unusable for these workloads and users must fall back to `minAvailable`. (See kubevirt/kubevirt#18063 for the downstream report.)

## Current behavior

`getExpectedScale` resolves only the direct `controllerRef` and attempts a single scale lookup against it. There is no traversal of the `ownerReferences` chain.

## Proposed enhancement

When the direct controller owner does not implement `/scale`, walk the `controllerRef` chain upward (`owner → owner-of-owner → …`) and use the **nearest ancestor that implements `/scale`** to compute `expectedPods`. Stop at the first scalable ancestor, or fall back to the current behavior if none exists.

Semantically this is correct: when many pods resolve to the same scalable ancestor (deduplicated by controller UID, as the controller already does), `expectedPods` becomes that ancestor's `scale.spec.replicas` — i.e. the real desired count of the workload the PDB is protecting.

### Open design questions (likely KEP material)

1. **Object lookups for intermediate owners.** Traversal requires GET-ing each intermediate owner object to read its `ownerReferences`. The disruption controller today only has typed finders for built-in workload types plus the polymorphic scale client. Walking arbitrary CRD chains needs a dynamic/metadata client and correspondingly broad RBAC. What is the right scoping (e.g. bounded depth, only follow `controller: true` refs)?
2. **Depth bound & cycle protection.** Cap traversal depth and guard against cyclic/malformed `ownerReferences`.
3. **Ambiguity.** If multiple matched pods resolve to *different* scalable ancestors, sum per-ancestor scales (the existing dedup-by-UID logic already handles this once ancestors are correctly identified).
4. **Backward compatibility.** Behavior only changes for pods whose direct owner is non-scalable today (currently a hard failure), so this is strictly an improvement — no regression for existing scalable-direct-owner cases.

## Alternatives considered

- **Implement `/scale` on the direct owner** (e.g. add it to the per-instance resource). Rejected as a general solution: it forces a `spec.replicas` field onto inherently-singleton resources and advertises horizontal scalability that does not exist, confusing HPA/`kubectl scale`/GitOps tooling.
- **Use `minAvailable`.** Works today and needs no change, but does not give users the `maxUnavailable` semantics they ask for. Acceptable workaround, not a fix.

## Environment

- Kubernetes: behavior confirmed from `pkg/controller/disruption/disruption.go` (`getExpectedScale`).

/sig apps
/kind feature

items.title: Job controller manageJob() returns active=0 during backoff, causing "cannot set more ready pods than active" status update rejection

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: sig/apps
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Apps.

labels.name: priority/important-longterm
labels.description: Important over the long term, but may not be staffed and/or may need multiple releases to complete.

labels.name: triage/accepted
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR is ready to be actively worked on.

items.body:
### What happened?

When the Job controller's `manageJob()` function determines that replacement pods are needed but a backoff timer is active (due to recent pod failures), it returns `active=0` to the caller. The caller uses this value to set `job.Status.Active=0` in a status update, while `job.Status.Ready` retains the real informer-computed count. The apiserver validation `RejectMoreReadyThanActivePods` (GA in 1.33 via `JobManagedBy`) correctly rejects this inconsistent update with 422.

Because the status update fails, the controller cannot:
- Flush `uncountedTerminatedPods`
- Remove `batch.kubernetes.io/job-tracking` finalizers from terminated pods

This causes pods to appear stuck in Terminating state and job status to become stale.

**Root cause:** Two locations in `manageJob()` return a hardcoded `0` instead of the real `active` count when backoff is active:

```go
// Location 1: global backoff
if remainingTime > 0 {
    jm.enqueueSyncJobWithDelay(logger, job, remainingTime)
    return 0, metrics.JobSyncActionPodsCreated, nil  // BUG: should be `active`
}

// Location 2: per-index backoff
if remainingTime > 0 {
    jm.enqueueSyncJobWithDelay(logger, job, remainingTime)
    return 0, metrics.JobSyncActionPodsCreated, nil  // BUG: should be `active`
}
```

The caller sets `job.Status.Active = active` (the returned 0), while `job.Status.Ready` stays at the informer count (e.g., 5). Result: `5 > 0` → 422.

The `0` was likely a "don't care" value from before `RejectMoreReadyThanActivePods` validation existed. Every other return path in `manageJob` returns the real active count.

### What did you expect to happen?

The backoff early-return in `manageJob()` should return the real active pod count (unchanged, since no pods were created or deleted), not 0.

Proposed fix:
```diff
     if remainingTime > 0 {
         jm.enqueueSyncJobWithDelay(logger, job, remainingTime)
-        return 0, metrics.JobSyncActionPodsCreated, nil
+        return active, metrics.JobSyncActionPodsCreated, nil
     }
```

Returning `active` (initialized at top of `manageJob` as `int32(len(jobCtx.activePods))`) means "I didn't create or delete any pods" — the correct semantics for a backoff deferral.


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

```bash
# 1. Create a Job
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: repro-ready-active
  namespace: default
spec:
  parallelism: 30
  completions: 30
  backoffLimit: 500
  completionMode: Indexed
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
      - name: worker
        image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.9
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "10m"
            memory: "16Mi"
EOF

# 2. Wait for all pods to be Running+Ready
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods -l job-name=repro-ready-active --timeout=120s

# 3. Force-delete 25 pods simultaneously
kubectl get pods -l job-name=repro-ready-active -o name | head -25 | \
  xargs -P25 kubectl delete --force --grace-period=0

# 4. Observe: job status is frozen, KCM logs show error
kubectl get job repro-ready-active -o jsonpath='active={.status.active} ready={.status.ready} failed={.status.failed}'
# Output: active=30 ready=30 failed=   (stale — doesn't reflect reality)

# KCM logs show:
# "Unhandled Error" err="syncing job: tracking status: adding uncounted pods to status:
#   Job.batch \"repro-ready-active\" is invalid: status.ready: Invalid value: 5:
#   cannot set more ready pods than active"

# 5. Bug self-resolves after ~10 min when backoff expires (if no new failures arrive)
```

### Anything else we need to know?

- The bug fires on any multi-pod Job that experiences a pod failure while other pods are still Ready. For single failures (10s backoff), it produces a few 422 errors that self-resolve. For mass failures (spot reclamation, node failure → backoff capped at 10 min), it causes visible stuck pods and stale status for the full backoff duration.
- No data loss occurs. The job eventually completes. The impact is operational: stuck Terminating pods, stale status, KCM error log spam.
- The `metrics.JobSyncActionPodsCreated` label on the return is also incorrect (no pods were created), but that's cosmetic.


### Kubernetes version

<details>

Bug present from 1.31 (when `RejectMoreReadyThanActivePods` was introduced, beta default-on) through latest master. Unconditional from 1.33 (`JobManagedBy` GA).

Tested and reproduced on 1.35.


</details>


### Cloud provider

<details>
AWS (EKS), but not cloud-specific. Reproducible on any cluster.
</details>


### OS version

N/A


### Install tools

N/A

items.body:
### What happened?

In 1.36 k8s graduated to Beta to feature gate: MutableSchedulingDirectivesForSuspendedJobs

The intention of the gate is to allow mutability of Job's scheduling directives whenever the Job is suspended. 

Previously the mutability was only allowed for Job which are "suspended" and "not started".

So, in principle the change is relaxation of conditions.

However, there is one specific scenario where the validation is stronger - for newly created Jobs for which we don't yet have the JobSuspended condition.

Here is the relevant code: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/registry/batch/job/strategy.go#L147-L155

I think we could fix the issue relatively simply be changing the mutability check into: `suspended && batchvalidation.IsConditionTrue(oldJob.Status.Conditions, batch.JobSuspended) && oldJob.Status.Active == 0` 

`suspended && (notStarted || batchvalidation.IsConditionTrue(oldJob.Status.Conditions, batch.JobSuspended)) && oldJob.Status.Active == 0`  - basically include the `notStarted` as an OR.

### What did you expect to happen?

This is discovered as it makes MultiKueue not working for K8s 1.36: https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kueue/pull/11576

This is because on the management cluster Kueue, when scheduling, attempts to inject scheduling directives to a Job which does not have the JobSuspended condition.

This can be workedaround in Kueue, but raising the point that the validation change in 1.36 is breaking.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a suspended Job managed by an external controller (as it happens when MultiKueue is used)
2. Then try to modify the Job's scheduling directives, eg inject nodeSelector while the Job is suspended (and never started)

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

items.body:
/sig apps
/kind feature

The DaemonSet controller reports aggregate counts without showing whether unavailable or not-yet-updated pods are on NotReady nodes.

## What would you like to be added?

Add a DaemonSet status signal that lets rollout automation distinguish between:

- pods unavailable because the new rollout is problematic and may need rollback, and
- pods unavailable because the underlying node is NotReady, shutting down, disconnected, or under maintenance.

The second case creates problems for automation. The exact solution is up for discussion, but having a status field such as `daemonset.status.numberUnavailableOnNotReadyNodes` would be useful.

The goal is not to make the DaemonSet controller own node repair or maintenance policy. It is to expose enough information for rollout controllers, Helm hooks, operators, and humans to interpret rollout status without reimplementing their own attribution logic.

## Why is this needed?

In large clusters, DaemonSet rollout status can be ambiguous when only a few pods remain unavailable.

Example DaemonSet status from a large cluster:

```yaml
updateStrategy:
  rollingUpdate:
    maxSurge: 0
    maxUnavailable: 10%
  type: RollingUpdate
status:
  currentNumberScheduled: 100
  desiredNumberScheduled: 100
  numberAvailable: 95
  numberMisscheduled: 0
  numberReady: 95
  numberUnavailable: 5
  observedGeneration: 10
  updatedNumberScheduled: 95
```

This DaemonSet is not blocked by `maxUnavailable`; with `desiredNumberScheduled: 100` and `maxUnavailable: 10%`, the rollout budget is 10 pods. However, external rollout verification still needs to answer:

Are the remaining 5 pods unavailable because the rollout is unhealthy, or because they are on NotReady nodes?

`numberUnavailable` alone cannot answer that. It may include pods affected by rollout issues, pod readiness, `minReadySeconds`, pending/rejected pods, terminating pods, old revisions, kubelet issues, or NotReady node state.

Today, automation has to inspect Pods and often list Nodes before deciding whether the rollout should pass. That has two practical costs:

1. Every rollout verifier or operator must implement its own attribution and ignore policy.
2. In large clusters, repeated rollout checks can create additional API server and etcd load, often during periods where node lifecycle events and DaemonSet rollouts are already increasing control-plane activity.

This is especially visible for DaemonSets with broad tolerations:

```yaml
tolerations:
- operator: Exists
```

For these DaemonSets, taints do not reduce the desired node set. A NotReady node may still be counted as desired, but `numberUnavailable` does not show whether NotReady nodes are the cause of the remaining unavailability. Consumers must inspect lower-level objects to attribute the reason.

## How can we reproduce it?

One possible reproduction:

1. Create a cluster with many nodes.
2. Create a DaemonSet with `RollingUpdate`, `maxSurge: 0`, and a non-zero `maxUnavailable`.
3. Give the DaemonSet broad tolerations, such as `operator: Exists`, so node taints do not exclude most nodes from `desiredNumberScheduled`.
4. Start a DaemonSet rollout.
5. Make a small number of nodes NotReady or disconnected while leaving the Node objects present.
6. Observe that DaemonSet status reports aggregate unavailable/not-updated counts, but does not indicate whether NotReady nodes account for those counts.
7. Observe that external rollout automation must inspect Pods and often LIST Nodes to decide whether the rollout should fail or be accepted.

## Current behavior

DaemonSet status reports aggregate scheduling, availability, and update counts. It does not show how many unavailable or not-yet-updated pods are on NotReady nodes.

## Expected behavior

Kubernetes should provide a supported way to identify DaemonSet rollout unavailability caused by NotReady nodes. This could be an API status enhancement, condition, event, or documentation update.

## Related issues

- https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/122912 - DaemonSet controller and Graceful Node Shutdown manager disagree when making workload placement decisions.
- https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/137895 - DaemonSet pod create/reject/delete loops during node deletion/shutdown.
- https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/117204 - DaemonSet rollout can be affected by nodes joining/leaving or becoming unavailable.
- https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/138240 - DaemonSet rollout can get stuck when the controller chooses bad nodes. This is related, but the scenario here is different: the rollout may not be stuck on `maxUnavailable`; the missing signal is how to interpret the remaining unavailable/not-updated pods.
- https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/112733 - Node lifecycle can leave pods misleadingly ready/running in some node state transitions.

items.title: ReplicaSet scale-down spreads pod deletions across nodes, preventing efficient node consolidation

labels.name: sig/apps
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Apps.

labels.name: needs-triage
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR lacks a `triage/foo` label and requires one.

items.body:
## What would you like to be added?

The ReplicaSet controller's pod deletion sort order during scale-down should have an option to concentrate deletions on nodes that are closest to empty, rather than spreading deletions evenly across nodes.

When a Deployment scales down, the RS controller's [sort order](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/replicaset/replica_set_utils.go) preferentially removes pods from nodes that have the most co-located replicas from the same owner. This spreads deletions across nodes. It maintains even replica distribution, but it works against node autoscalers like Karpenter and cluster-autoscaler, which need empty or nearly-empty nodes to reclaim compute with minimal additional pod disruption.

**Example:**

5 nodes, each running 4 pods from one Deployment (20 replicas total). HPA scales down to 10.

| | Today (spreading) | With consolidation-aware deletion |
|---|---|---|
| Pods removed per node | 2, 2, 2, 2, 2 | 4, 4, 2, 0, 0 |
| Empty nodes after scale-down | 0 | 2 |
| Additional evictions needed | Yes, autoscaler must evict more pods to consolidate | None, 2 nodes can be removed immediately |
| Total pod disruptions | 10 (scale-down) + N (consolidation) | 10 (scale-down only) |

The same 10 pods are deleted in both cases. The difference is *which* pods. Concentrating deletions on fewer nodes produces empty nodes that the autoscaler can remove without additional disruption.

**Proposed approach:** A feature-gated change to the RS controller's pod deletion sort order that prefers pods on nodes with fewer total active pods (consolidation-friendly), as an alternative to the current spreading behavior. This is tracked in [kubernetes/enhancements#5982](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/5982).

This issue is part of a broader discussion on coordinating workload scale-in with node autoscaling. See the [community discussion document](https://docs.google.com/document/d/193Fx7and-DitsGG1ly9-r1f26wmux5gMG8N3G-jPjZU/) and the [Node Lifecycle Management use cases document](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1EINvuVzEoRra0CKH6uQnOcQJVbd7ZnxT1bcyySN-r7c/) (use case 5) for the full context.

**Related work:**
- [kubernetes/enhancements#5982](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/5982): KEP for RS controller consolidation heuristic, currently on-hold
- [#107598](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/107598): Configurable down-scaling behaviour in ReplicaSets (closed, predecessor proposal)
- [#123541](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/123541): Extend scale subresource to support pod-deletion-cost (closed, predecessor proposal)
- [KEP-2255](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/2255): Pod Deletion Cost (existing annotation mechanism)
- [Karpenter Pod Deletion Cost Controller RFC](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/karpenter/pull/2935): Autoscaler-side approach using annotations

## Why is this needed?

The ReplicaSet controller and node autoscalers optimize for different goals independently. The RS controller spreads pod deletions to maintain even distribution. The autoscaler needs pods concentrated on fewer nodes so it can remove empty ones. These goals conflict during scale-down, and the result is unnecessary pod disruption.

The timing makes this hard to fix after the fact. Pod scale-in happens first: the RS controller picks which pods to delete. Then the autoscaler reacts, notices underutilized nodes, and evicts more pods to consolidate. By that point, the spreading has already happened. Better consolidation afterward helps, but it cannot undo the suboptimal deletions.

This affects any cluster that uses both HPA and a node autoscaler. The impact scales with the frequency of scale-down events and the number of replicas. Clusters with diurnal traffic patterns, frequent deployments, or bursty workloads hit this repeatedly.

The `controller.kubernetes.io/pod-deletion-cost` annotation (KEP-2255) lets external controllers influence deletion order, but annotations must be set before scale-down starts and create API server write load proportional to pod count. A native RS controller heuristic avoids both problems: it uses information already in the informer cache and requires no external coordination.

### What happened?

When creating a Job (e.g. `completions: 4`, `parallelism: 1`), the Job's STATUS column in `kubectl get job` shows `Running` even though all of its pods are in `Pending` state.

```console
$ kubectl create -f sleep-job.yaml
job.batch/sleep-job created

$ kubectl get job
NAME        STATUS    COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
sleep-job   Running   0/1 of 4      3s         3s

$ kubectl get pods
NAME                         READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
sleep-job-5lp4b              0/1     Pending   0          9s
sleep-job-b2kvh              0/1     Pending   0          9s
sleep-job-h7pt4              0/1     Pending   0          9s
sleep-job-rdnlc              0/1     Pending   0          9s
test-nginx-9496d7c6b-2dp67   1/1     Running   0          30h
test-nginx-9496d7c6b-pwfbc   1/1     Running   0          30h
```

The Job status is misleading — it reports `Running` when no pods are actually running (all are `Pending`).

### What did you expect to happen?

The Job STATUS should reflect that no pods are currently running. When all pods are in `Pending` state, the Job status should not show `Running`. A status like `Pending` or `Suspended` (or a new status that distinguishes "created but not yet scheduled") would be more accurate.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a Job manifest with `completions: 4` where pods will remain `Pending` (e.g., due to insufficient resources, unschedulable nodes, or a simple sleep Job on a cluster with limited capacity):

```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: sleep-job
spec:
  completions: 4
  parallelism: 1
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: sleep
        image: busybox
        command: ["sleep", "3600"]
      restartPolicy: Never
```

2. Apply the manifest: `kubectl create -f sleep-job.yaml`
3. Observe Job status: `kubectl get job`
4. Observe pod status: `kubectl get pods`
5. Note that the Job shows `Running` while all pods show `Pending`.

### Anything else we need to know?

This can be confusing for users debugging scheduling issues, since the Job status suggests work is actively running when it is not.

1. The Stackable Operator for Trino (`trino-op` from now on) creates two `StatefulSet` objects with a single replica. They both expose the same problem, so for simplicity, I will use only one of them from now on (`trino-coordinator-default`).
2. The initial revision of this sts is `trino-coordinator-default-5f5598d4c8`. This first STS  revision has a faulty command args  and can never become available.
3. The `trino-op` updates the sts rapidly to the revision `trino-coordinator-default-787556ff59`. Now the STS command args are correct and the pods should be able to become ready.
4. The pod created initially is never updated so it never becomes ready.

To summarize my understanding, the sts revision is never updated if the pod never becomes ready, and the pod doesn't become ready because it has an old revision.

In the logs you see that `currentRevision` is never the same as `updateRevision`:


The pod should become ready according to the `updateRevision` of the sts.

### Which jobs are flaking?

`pull-kubernetes-unit` ([Prow log](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/pr-logs/pull/137336/pull-kubernetes-unit/2028488280995008512))

### Which tests are flaking?

`TestStalePodDisruption/stale_pod_disruption` in `k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/controller/disruption`

### Since when has it been flaking?

Observed on 2025-03-02 in PR https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/137336. This is a recurrence of https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/112594 (closed 2022-09-21).

### Testgrid link

N/A (observed in presubmit)

### Reason for failure (if possible)

The test creates a pod with a `DisruptionTarget=True` condition (no `DeletionTimestamp`), advances the fake clock past the 2-minute `stalePodDisruptionTimeout`, adds the pod to the indexer, and then polls for the controller to set `DisruptionTarget=False`. The poll times out after 30 seconds:

```
=== RUN   TestStalePodDisruption/stale_pod_disruption
    disruption_test.go:1560: Failed waiting for worker to sync: timed out waiting for the condition, (-want,+got):
          []v1.PodCondition{
              {
                  Type:               "DisruptionTarget",
                  ObservedGeneration: 0,
        -         Status:             "False",
        +         Status:             "True",
                  LastProbeTime:      {},
                  ... // 1 ignored and 2 identical fields
              },
          }
--- FAIL: TestStalePodDisruption/stale_pod_disruption (30.01s)
```

**Race condition analysis:** The test starts the controller with `go dc.Run(tCtx)` ([disruption_test.go:1543](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/disruption/disruption_test.go#L1543)) and then immediately adds the pod to the informer indexer ([disruption_test.go:1548](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/disruption/disruption_test.go#L1548)). The flow for stale pod cleanup is:

1. `addPod` event handler calls `nonTerminatingPodHasStaleDisruptionCondition()` to check if the condition is stale
2. If stale, it enqueues the pod into `stalePodDisruptionQueue` via `enqueueStalePodDisruptionCleanup()` with `AddAfter(key, d)`
3. The `stalePodDisruptionWorker` goroutine picks it up and calls `syncStalePodDisruption()`
4. `syncStalePodDisruption()` patches the pod condition to `False`

The flake occurs because:
- There is no synchronization ensuring the controller's `Run()` goroutine has fully started and its informer event handlers are registered before the pod is added to the indexer
- The `addPod` event may fire before the informer caches have synced (line 476), or the `stalePodDisruptionWorker` goroutine (line 487) may not yet be running
- The pod is added directly to the indexer (`GetIndexer().Add()`) rather than through the informer's normal flow, which may bypass event delivery depending on timing
- Since the fake clock is advanced *before* the pod is added (line 1547), the `nonTerminatingPodHasStaleDisruptionCondition` check correctly computes `waitFor=0`, but if the event is missed entirely, the cleanup never gets enqueued

### Anything else we need to know?

This is a recurrence of https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/112594, which was closed in September 2022. The underlying race condition between controller startup and pod indexer insertion appears to still exist.

/sig apps

labels.name: kind/bug

items.body:
### What happened?

When a DaemonSet is created, the DaemonSet controller attempts to create the required Pods on each node. However, if the initial Pod creation is interrupted (e.g., a Mutating Admission Webhook adds a deletionTimestamp immediately after creation), the Pod enters the terminating state before it can be fully scheduled or observed as running.

In this case, the DaemonSet controller observes the deletion event and calls:

`dsc.expectations.DeletionObserved(logger, dsKey)`
(see code: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b236451928797b544423a73bfb67b6846178e3b1/pkg/controller/daemon/daemon_controller.go#L530)

This satisfies the expectation for that particular Pod, but no new Pod creation is triggered because the controller only attempts to create missing Pods during full reconciliation (e.g., when the DaemonSet spec changes or the controller resyncs). If the DaemonSet object itself remains unchanged, the controller will not attempt to create a replacement Pod, even though the previous Pod was never successfully running.

As a result, the DaemonSet can remain in a broken state with fewer Pods than desired, and the missing Pods are never recreated.



### What did you expect to happen?

The DaemonSet controller should continue attempting to create new Pods to satisfy the desired number of replicas on each node, even if the initial Pod creation was interrupted and the Pod was immediately terminated (e.g., by a webhook setting deletionTimestamp).

Ideally, the controller should treat such a case similarly to a failed Pod creation or a Pod that was deleted before becoming ready — and trigger a new creation attempt.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a Mutating Admission Webhook that adds a deletionTimestamp to every newly created Pod (for demonstration purposes only).

-  Example: a simple webhook that patches /metadata/deletionTimestamp with metav1.Now() on CREATE operations.

2. Create a DaemonSet (any simple DaemonSet, e.g., using busybox image with a sleep command).
3. Observe that:

- The webhook immediately adds deletionTimestamp to the Pod.

- The Pod enters Terminating state and is deleted.

- The DaemonSet controller observes the deletion and calls DeletionObserved(), satisfying the expectation.

- No new Pod is ever created on that node, even though the DaemonSet still has missing replicas.

### Anything else we need to know?

1. This behavior occurs because the DaemonSet controller relies heavily on the expectations mechanism to avoid over- or under-creation. When a deletion is observed, it clears the expectation without triggering a new creation attempt unless the DaemonSet object is updated or the periodic resync occurs.

2. We believe there should be a safety mechanism to handle abnormal cases like this (e.g., webhook-induced immediate termination). One possible solution is:

- After expectations expire (TTL) or when a deletion is observed without the Pod ever being ready, force a reconciliation to attempt creating a new Pod.

- Alternatively, track whether the Pod was ever in a "running" or "scheduled" state before deletion, and if not, treat it as a failed creation and retry.

labels.name: kind/bug

items.body:
### What happened?

When a StatefulSet has `minReadySeconds` configured, the `completeRollingUpdate` function prematurely marks the rolling update as complete. It sets `status.CurrentRevision = status.UpdateRevision` as soon as all replicas are Ready, without waiting for them to be Available (i.e., Ready for at least `minReadySeconds`).

### What did you expect to happen?

The rolling update should not be considered complete until all replicas are both Ready and Available (have been Ready for at least minReadySeconds).

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a StatefulSet with minReadySeconds set to a non-zero value (e.g., 60s)
2. Trigger a rolling update
3. Observe that status.CurrentRevision is updated to status.UpdateRevision before pods have been Available for at least minReadySeconds

### Anything else we need to know?

Root cause:

In function [completeRollingUpdate](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.35.0/pkg/controller/statefulset/stateful_set_utils.go#L638-L647), the condition checks ReadyReplicas but not AvailableReplicas:

```go
func completeRollingUpdate(set *apps.StatefulSet, status *apps.StatefulSetStatus) {
	if set.Spec.UpdateStrategy.Type == apps.RollingUpdateStatefulSetStrategyType &&
		status.UpdatedReplicas == *set.Spec.Replicas &&
		status.ReadyReplicas == *set.Spec.Replicas &&
		status.Replicas == *set.Spec.Replicas {
		status.CurrentReplicas = status.UpdatedReplicas
		status.CurrentRevision = status.UpdateRevision
	}
}
```


The fix is to add status.AvailableReplicas == *set.Spec.Replicas to the condition. This was originally identified in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/122272#discussion_r1526750533.

Kubernetes version: all versions since StatefulSetMinReadySeconds graduated to GA (v1.27+)

items.body:
The `selector.matchLabels` field was made immutable some years back and since then I've just seen so much friction for users dealing with this part of the spec.

Mostly because people just copy other labels, such as org data (as [suggested in the docs](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/labels/#motivation)) into `matchLabels`, then later need to change those label values and are then faced with a resource they cannot update due to the dreaded `field is immutable` error. There are solutions for this, e.g.deleting a deployment with the `--cascade=orphan` option, but this is risky and messy. We just faced an incident where the newly orphaned replicaset was adopted by another deployment and scaled down.

This leads me to question why does this field even exist in the spec? In what world are people wanting to manually specify the relationship between parent/child resources?

Currently, some components in Kubernetes have been migrated (or partially migrated) to [contextual logging](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/master/keps/sig-instrumentation/3077-contextual-logging/README.md). However, an incorrect pattern was introduced during the migration: Error-level logs are being called with verbosity methods (e.g., .V()).

The underlying package go-logr/logr, which contextual logging relies on, ignores the verbosity level when printing Error-level logs. For example, in the statement `logger.V(8).Error(nil, "Readiness probe already exists for container", "pod", klog.KObj(pod), "containerName", c.Name)`, the error log will be printed regardless of the verbosity level set.

This can lead to error log flooding, which may hinder users' ability to review normal logs for troubleshooting. More critically, according to the [Kubernetes logging policy](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/contributors/devel/sig-instrumentation/logging.md#what-method-to-use), logs should only be recorded when the information requires action from an administrator. This directly contradicts the practice of setting verbosity levels for Error logs, as administrators using the default logging level might miss these actionable errors. items.body:
### What happened?

When a Deployment is scaled down during an in-progress rolling update (with maxSurge=0),
  the deployment controller gets stuck in an infinite loop and the rolling update never completes.

  The issue occurs because:
  1. During a rolling update, ReplicaSet annotations (deployment.kubernetes.io/desired-replicas)
     are set to the initial deployment size
  2. If the deployment is scaled down while the update is in progress, the replica count changes
     but the annotations remain stale
  3. isScalingEvent() detects the annotation mismatch and returns true, causing the controller
     to call sync() instead of rolloutRolling()
  4. scale() checks if replica counts match and returns early without updating annotations
     (lines 303-304 in pkg/controller/deployment/sync.go)
  5. scaleReplicaSetAndRecordEvent() also has an early return when replicas match (lines 400-401)
  6. The annotations are never updated, creating an infinite loop

  This prevents the rolling update from proceeding. Pods remain on the old version indefinitely, and there are no error messages.

  **Impact:** Applications cannot be updated, security patches cannot be deployed, and the
  deployment appears healthy while being completely stuck.

### What did you expect to happen?

The deployment controller should update ReplicaSet annotations even when replica counts
  already match the desired state. After scaling during a rolling update, the controller should:

  1. Detect the annotation mismatch
  2. Update the stale annotations to match the current deployment.spec.replicas
  3. Continue with the rolling update by calling rolloutRolling()
  4. Create a new ReplicaSet with the updated template
  5. Complete the rolling update successfully

  The annotations should be kept in sync with deployment.spec.replicas regardless of whether
  the replica count changed, to ensure isScalingEvent() correctly identifies true scaling
  events versus stale annotation states.

labels.name: kind/bug

items.body:
### What happened?

`controller.ComputeHash` method ([ref](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/6eee830d4fa0cdb7d75dac4b3b4d22d639dce54b/pkg/controller/controller_utils.go#L1395)) used to get the hash of PodTemplateSpec (used by daemonset and deployment controllers) can return shorter hash than expected 10 chars, depending on the `PodTemplateSpec` that is passed to this func. Some users might rely on specific length of the hash that is appended to the `ReplicaSet` or `ControllerRevision` names.

/sig apps

### What did you expect to happen?

The hash to be of the exact same length regardless of PodTemplateSpec used.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

I found this during Workload API implementation (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/134564). Adding a new field to the pod spec changed the hash in the tests. Manipulating with the labels can lead to correct or incorrect hash length (see https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/134564#discussion_r2439332948).

### Anything else we need to know?

ComputeHash is encoding the hash number (`podTemplateSpecHasher.Sum32()`) into the string using `rand.SafeEncodeString`. When this issue occurs, the hash number has 9 digits, not 10, what leads to the shorter hash.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/6eee830d4fa0cdb7d75dac4b3b4d22d639dce54b/pkg/controller/controller_utils.go#L1395-L1406

items.body:
### What happened?

I have a kubernetes operator, which "relied" on the pre 1.34 behavior of STS that accepted an invalid VolumeClaimTemplate. This way, I could create the PVCs myself, for example with different storageClasses, while still utilizing StatefulSet operation, update strategy, etc. Now, with an STS with a fixed volumeClaimTemplate, I still can pre-create the PVCs, howewer, changing a PVC's storageclass (by deleting and recreating with another) wont work anymore, as STS controller will immediately create one with correct specs in volumeClaimTemplate.

### What did you expect to happen?

It would be nice that [this](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/132212) change had been gated with a FeatureGate.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

With, pre 1.34 this statefulset could be created:

```
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: test
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: test
  serviceName: test
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: test
    spec:
      containers:
      - image: test
        name: test
        volumeMounts:
        - mountPath: /test
          name: data
  volumeClaimTemplates:
  - apiVersion: v1
    kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
    metadata:
      name: data
```

With 1.34, this is not accepted anymore.



### Anything else we need to know?

Right now, before StatefulSet creation, I already can pre-create the PVCs, so at the end we may observe incosistencies, as actual PVCs might differ from what the volumeClaimTemplate holds. Following this, either we should deny pre-created PVCs at all, or relax restrictions a bit, and perhaps allow the user to create the PVCs himself. Perhaps, with a totally empty `spec` field in volumeClaimTemplate.

items.body:
### What would you like to be added?

1. Background Description
We have some pods that require long-lived connections. However, when the nodes hosting these pods restart or due to deployment sequencing issues, a large number of requests are sent to the pods that become ready first, resulting in highly uneven load distribution.

2. Current Situation
Currently, there are mechanisms like readinessGates that provide control over when a pod is ready to serve external traffic. However, this requires additional specific configurations and does not seem very convenient to use.

3. Proposal
Can we implement a controller similar to the successPolicy strategy used in Jobs? For example, defining how many replicas under the controller must be ready before the pods can serve external traffic, thereby addressing the load imbalance caused by sequential startup.

Alternatively, are there other approaches that could meet this need?

### Why is this needed?

Support rules for defining when controller replicas become available

items.body:
### What would you like to be added?

GetPodFromTemplate currently drops any ownerReferences specified in the pod template:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f28b4c9efbca5c5c0af716d9f2d5702667ee8a45/pkg/controller/controller_utils.go#L575-L582

This means that workload authors do not have a generic way to establish belongs-to relationships between the eventual pods and other objects.

### Why is this needed?

Controllers / schedulers can require visibility to connections from higher-level ancestor objects grouping sets of related pods.

There are implications to propagating owner references we would need to think through and derisk:
* if controllerRef is nil and all template.OwnerReferences are missing, new pods would get GCed immediately
* if controllerRef is non-nil, and template.OwnerReferences has a `isController:true`, pod creation would fail validation
* if controllerRef is non-nil and the controller was counting on generic GC to clean up pods, it would now wait until all template.OwnerReferences are gone too

/sig api-machinery
/sig apps
cc @erictune

### What would you like to be added?

The suggestion is to add a `lastFailureTime` to mimics the `lastSuccessfulTime`, that is updated when a job has the JobFailure condition.

#### Alternative

An alternative would be to have Conditions for the CronJob that gives more information on the last job result, and for which generation the job was created, but this seems like a bigger refactor.

### Why is this needed?

It is currently hard to know if a CronJob last execution was successful or a failure. We can usually check for `if status.lastSuccessfulTime < status.lastScheduledTime`, then assume it is a failure, but as soon as a new Job is scheduled, we lose the information to know if the last one failed or not.

items.body:
**What happened:**

When modifying only metadata (labels or annotations) in a StatefulSet's pod template spec, the StatefulSet controller unnecessarily recreates all pods, causing service disruption for workloads that are otherwise healthy and functioning correctly.

**What you expected to happen:**

Changes to pod metadata (labels/annotations) in the StatefulSet template should be applied directly to existing pods without recreation, similar to how kubectl can directly modify pod labels/annotations without restart.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible):**

1. Create a StatefulSet with 3 replicas:
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: test-sts
spec:
  replicas: 3
  serviceName: test-svc
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: test
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: test
        version: v1
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:1.20
```

2. Wait for all pods to be Running
3. Update only the metadata in the template:
```bash
kubectl patch statefulset test-sts -p '{"spec":{"template":{"metadata":{"labels":{"version":"v2"}}}}}'
```

4. This triggers the StatefulSet controller to recreate pods one by one due to template hash change

**Anything else we need to know?:**

This is the documented behavior of StatefulSets where any template change triggers a rolling update based on template hash comparison. However, this creates operational challenges:
- Production workloads suffer unnecessary downtime when adding operational labels (monitoring, alerting, compliance tags)
- The same metadata changes can be applied directly to pods using `kubectl label` or `kubectl annotate` without restart
- This creates inconsistent behavior where direct pod updates work fine but template updates cause recreation
- Forces operators to choose between:
  - Accept downtime for metadata changes
  - Use direct pod modification (which gets overwritten on future updates)
  - Use external operators/controllers to manage pod metadata, which is actually an anti-pattern to have more than one controller manage the pods.

**Additional Context:**

This enhancement would:
1. Reduce operational overhead when managing StatefulSet metadata
2. Improve availability for stateful services
3. Align StatefulSet behavior with the principle that metadata-only changes shouldn't require pod recreation
4. Provide consistency with how direct pod label/annotation modifications work

**Question for Maintainers:**
Is restarting pods for metadata-only changes a conscious design decision? If so, what's the reasoning behind it - implementation simplicity, consistency guarantees, or specific technical concerns?

labels.name: kind/bug

items.body:
### What happened?

During rollout of a Deployment with a `rollingUpdate` strategy (`maxSurge: 3`, `maxUnavailable: 0`) and `podAntiAffinity` based on `pod-template-hash`, the Kubernetes Scheduler does not take the `pod-deletion-cost` annotation into account. This leads to an imbalance where two pods with different `pod-template-hash` values are scheduled on the same node for an extended period. Specifically, the Scheduler should prioritize scheduling on nodes with existing pods of lower-cost pods in a manner that maintains a balanced distribution across nodes.

For example, in a setup with 6 replicas across 6 nodes, when a rollout begins, new pods are scheduled alongside existing ones without considering their deletion costs, resulting in a situation with two pods on one node and none on others, thus leading to an undesired imbalance throughout the rollout.


### What did you expect to happen?

I expected that the Scheduler would take `pod-deletion-cost` into account when scheduling new replicas during a rollout, ensuring that it removes lower-cost pods first and maintains balanced distribution across nodes to comply with `podAntiAffinity` rules.


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a Deployment with the following configuration:
    ```yaml
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    metadata:
      name: foo
    spec:
      replicas: 6
      selector:
        matchLabels:
          app: foo
      template:
        metadata:
          labels:
            app: foo
        spec:
          affinity:
            podAntiAffinity:
              requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
              - labelSelector:
                  matchExpressions:
                  - key: app.kubernetes.io/name
                    operator: In
                    values:
                    - foo
                matchLabelKeys:
                - pod-template-hash
                topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
          containers:
          - name: foo
            image: foo:latest
    ```
2. Annotate the pods with pod-deletion-cost as shown below:
```
| node   | pod  | pod-template-hash | pod-deletion-cost | Zone       |
| NodeA1 | pod1 | foo-123           | 999               | us-west-2a | 
| NodeB1 | pod2 | foo-123           | 999               | us-west-2b |
| NodeC1 | pod3 | foo-123           | 999               | us-west-2c |
| NodeA2 | pod4 | foo-123           | 998               | us-west-2a | 
| NodeB2 | pod5 | foo-123           | 998               | us-west-2b |
| NodeC2 | pod6 | foo-123           | 998               | us-west-2c |
```

3. Do a rollout restart, it surges and it could do the following:
```
| node   | pod  | pod-template-hash | pod-deletion-cost | Zone       |
| NodeA1 | pod1 | foo-123           | 999               | us-west-2a | 
| NodeA1 | pod7 | foo-124           | <not-set-yet>     | us-west-2a | 
| NodeB1 | pod2 | foo-123           | 999               | us-west-2b |
| NodeB1 | pod8 | foo-124           | <not-set-yet>     | us-west-2b |
| NodeC1 | pod3 | foo-123           | 999               | us-west-2c |
| NodeA2 | pod4 | foo-123           | 998               | us-west-2a | 
| NodeB2 | pod5 | foo-123           | 998               | us-west-2b |
| NodeC2 | pod6 | foo-123           | 998               | us-west-2c |
| NodeC2 | pod9 | foo-124           | <not-set-yet>     | us-west-2c |
```

This will put two pods (with different pod-template-hash) onto the same node, but take down the pods with lower cost, leading to:

```
| node   | pod  | pod-template-hash | pod-deletion-cost | Zone       |
| NodeA1 | pod1 | foo-123           | 999               | us-west-2a |
| NodeA1 | pod7 | foo-124           | <not-set-yet>     | us-west-2a |  
| NodeB1 | pod2 | foo-123           | 999               | us-west-2b |
| NodeB1 | pod8 | foo-124           | <not-set-yet>     | us-west-2b |
| NodeC1 | pod3 | foo-123           | 999               | us-west-2c |
| NodeA2 |      |                   |                   | us-west-2a | 
| NodeB2 |      |                   |                   | us-west-2b |
| NodeC2 | pod9 | foo-124           | <not-set-yet>     | us-west-2c |
```

### Anything else we need to know?

- The current behavior gives rise to an imbalance in pod distribution across nodes, ultimately leading to resource underutilization in some zones while overloading others. 
- This issue seems particularly problematic in configurations where there's a custom tooling that adds pod-deletion-cost to workloads

### What would you like to be added?

The doc for [Daemonset](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/manage-daemon/update-daemon-set/) only mentioned that maxSurge and maxAvailable cannot be both 0. maxSurge and maxUnavailable is supported for [Deployment](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment/#max-surge), and there is no obvious reason why this option cannot be supported. 

### Why is this needed?

We want the same granular control of Daemonset like Deployment.
